newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions press new left government on wages.
newsitem.headline: French unions press new left government on wages.

text.p: Trade unions told France's incoming left-wing government on Tuesday that they would press for higher salaries and fairer distribution of national wealth after voters turned their back on the right and economic austerity.

The leaders of unions ranging from the Communist-led CGT to the white-collar CGC said they would make their demands at a "national conference" which Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has promised on jobs, wages and work organisation.

Jospin, who took over from Alain Juppe as prime minister on Tuesdaym and plans to form a new left-wing government this week, has set himself a target of creating 700,000 jobs in the next couple of years and reducing the work week to 35 hours from 39.

CGT leader Louis Viannet said he wanted the national minimum wage raised beyond an automatic index-linked increase in July and said wage-earners should not wait on the outcome of Jospin's jobs conference to campaign for higher pay at company level.

Nicole Notat, who has carved herself an image as consensual leader of the traditionally Socialist-leaning CFDT union, urged Jospin to reopen talks on pay for several million civil servants after a two-year freeze by Juppe's centre-right coalition.
She took a less radical line than the CGT on work time, warning that the CFDT was too attached to a reduction in work time to seek overly hasty government action.

Marc Vilbenoit, leader of the white-collar CGC, said he was counting on the jobs conference, which will include employers and unions, to overhaul work-time organisation and ensure that productivity gains produced greater payoffs for salary earners who had consistently been left behind as company profits rose.

Viannet, whose CGT union dominates the 180,000-strong SNCF railways but is also present in other public sector and civil service ranks, called on France Inter radio for a "very quick" rise in the minimum wage and also said he wanted privatisations halted, notably the sale of a stake in France Telecom.

In marked contrast, CFDT union leader Notat said she was not hostile to the France Telecom sale and instead stressed the need for fresh negotiations on civil service pay and on achieving a carefully-planned move towards a 35-hour week.

"Things have fallen behind in this domain. Civil servants have had their purchasing power frozen for two years. This cannot go on for ever. Public service negotiations should be reopened," she told Europe 1 radio.

Vilbenoit, whose smaller CGC union is almost solely active in the private sector, told Reuters that salaries had borne the brunt for too long under successive governments while corporate and capital income profits reaped an increasing share of gains in productivity.
"We should be able to develop some form of mechanism...which would adjust the balance between wages, capital income, jobs and work time," he said in a telephone interview.
"We will present proposals on upgrading salaries, on the negotiation of pay scales and on pushing for a reduction in working time based on new forms of work reorganisation."
"The civil service has fallen behind but I can assure you that the story is just the same in the private sector," he said.

Outgoing civil service minister Dominique Perben unilaterally imposed a civil service pay offer in February, angering unions who said the increase of 2.8 percent over 1997 and 1998 failed to keep up with inflation and, above all, did nothing to make up for pay freezes in the preceding years.
Unions called a one-day strike in the wake of that pay offer but failed to muster heavy support or generate anything like the fervous or public sector strikes back in 1995.

Some analysts say that weak strike and protest mobilisation over the past year is probably as much due to resignation and insecurity at a time of record 12.8 percent unemployment as it is to any disaffection with trade union campaigning.
